title: How Food Tasters Work
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore the job of professional food tasting, opening with a bit of banter about Ben and Jerry's flavor gurus, Bob Ross, and listener Aaron Cooper. They cover the two routes into food tasting (degree-trained professionals versus everyday people hired after screening), sensory acuity testing by firms such as MMR Research Worldwide, and Schwan's in Marshall, Minnesota. A reported account of a temp taster who spent months testing frozen French fries, along with a Vice roundup of tasters (ice cream, pies, noodles), describes the monotonous, repetitive work, including rules like not smoking within thirty minutes of tasting. They discuss pay, pet food tasting, and the history of royal food tasters (Egyptians, Reagan-era US presidents, Putin, and a claim about Hitler's taster). Next comes a segment on training your palate: slowing down and savoring food, paying attention while eating, medications that alter taste, trying new foods, palate cleansers like citrus and sorbet, salt use, and a week without salt or sugar. The episode closes with listener mail from Chelsea about Butte, Montana, and the show's social media sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Bob Ross and dream-squashing, then chat about Aaron Cooper's Photoshop work and Ben and Jerry's flavor gurus and ice cream graveyard.

segments.title: Two paths into food tasting
segments.summary: Food tasting can be a professional career requiring a food science degree or training, or an everyday person can apply. Sensory acuity is needed, and firms like MMR Research Worldwide and Schwan in Marshall, Minnesota hire tasters after testing.

segments.title: Market research tasting panels
segments.summary: The hosts describe their own experiences in market research sessions testing products like Heineken and Home Depot items, and how tasting panels ask for specific ratings.

segments.title: Mayonnaise and a taster's daily grind
segments.summary: Chuck summarizes a Vice interview with a taster named Matthew who discusses mayonnaise, and the hosts discuss mayonnaise preferences, Duke's, and Miracle Whip.

segments.title: Frozen French fry testing and tasters' working days
segments.summary: A temp taster spent months testing frozen French fries, developing mouth sores from salt. Vice interviews describe ice cream tasting at Louise Vamber's job, Peter Nixon's pie tasting day at Morrison's, and a noodle taster's company.

segments.title: Taster rules, dental issues, and smoking
segments.summary: Tasters avoid smoking within thirty minutes of tasting and keep senses sharp. The hosts discuss dental trouble and whether smokers or people with allergies could be niche tasters, including portable gluten detectors.

segments.title: Milk, gluten, and local food
segments.summary: The hosts discuss gluten avoidance, differences in American milk, and buying local, organic, grass-fed milk and farm eggs.

segments.title: Taster pay and pet food tasting
segments.summary: Pay figures are unclear since the Bureau of Labor Statistics has no food taster category, only food scientists. Pet food is tasted by humans too, mainly for smell.

segments.title: History of royal food tasters
segments.summary: Royal food tasters date back to the Egyptians. Tasting protected against poison little, since few poisons act quickly enough. Secret Service presidential tasters, Putin's 2012 coverage, and a claim about Hitler's young female tasters are discussed.

segments.title: Developing your palate
segments.summary: Tips for a more sophisticated palate: slowing down, savoring, paying attention while eating, sitting down, and tasting apple slices. Attention improves digestion and helps avoid overeating. Some medications dull taste.

segments.title: Adventurous eating, palate cleansers, and salt
segments.summary: Hosts discuss trying new foods such as tongue and cheeks, palate cleansers like citrus and sorbet, salting onions in guacamole, finishing salt, and a week without salt or sugar to reset taste.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Chelsea from Butte, Montana writes about the town's history and identity. The hosts thank her and give social media and contact information.
